column2: Some portents give death, some fear from enemies; from the middle, fear, fame, death, loss, glory, happiness or unhappiness;
lordship and loss of wealth; and a honeycomb-covered anthill. In all such portents, O best of Brahmins,
one should carefully perform the auspicious peace rite by the rule laid down in the Kalpa. Thus astrology has been told to you in brief, O Brahmin.
After this I shall tell the unsurpassed science of metre.
Five groups of four moras (ganas) are declared, approved by the Arya metre and others. A syllable followed by a conjunct, visarga or anusvara is long relative to a short one.
It makes a short into a long: "go" is long, "la" is short. A foot is a quarter; a pause is called a caesura (yati).
Metre is equal, half-equal or unequal, O Narada. When the four feet have like characteristics, it is called equal.
Where the first and third, second and fourth are alike it is half-equal; where the four feet have different marks, it is unequal.
Beginning from one syllable and increasing one syllable at a time up to twenty-six syllables, the foot is separate for each.
Beyond that, the long-metres (dandakas) such as Chandavrishti are devised. With three or six feet there are gathas; hear the names in order.
Ukta, Atyukta, Madhya, Pratishtha, Supratishtha, Gayatri, Ushnih, Anushtubh, Brihati, Pankti,
Trishtubh, Jagati, Atijagati, Shakvari, Atishakvari, Ashti, Atyashti are remembered;
Dhriti, Atidhriti (Vidhriti), Kriti, Prakriti, Akriti, Vikriti, Samkriti, Atikriti, Utkriti:
these are the names of the metres, divided by the permutations (prastara). In a foot all long, having placed the first short below the long,
the rest is placed as above, ahead as before. This permutation is declared until all becomes short.
To find a lost number: if half is taken, if even then short; if odd, add one and half; for the stated, doubling from the first...
having reduced the places set in the short, they declare the number (as the ancients say). The syllables arising from the metre, from top to bottom,
from one in order, one should place above one; he should stop at the penultimate, dropping one from the top.
From the top, from the first long, thus operations with one, two and so on of the short-long; the sum of the numbers in the short-long operation gives the mixed number.
The sum of the stated numbers, plus one, produces this; the number itself, doubled and less one, is called the "path" (adhva) by the good.
Thus some characteristics of the metres have been told; the names of the varieties told in the permutation enter into them.
Having thus received the boon, the god Vyasa, son of Satyavati, took the fire-stick (arani) and churned it, wishing to make fire.
Then the divine sage saw an Apsara named Ghritachi, O Brahmin, bearing supreme beauty with her own radiance.
Seeing that Apsara, suddenly deluded by desire, the lord Vyasa, O lord of sages, in that forest became (agitated).
She, seeing Vyasa's mind agitated by desire, became a lovely she-parrot and approached, Ghritachi.
Seeing the Apsara covered in another form, followed by the king of love in all his limbs,
the sage greatly restraining the desire in his heart could not control his mind, which had flown out.
Because of what was to be, and by Ghritachi's body, his mind was carried off, though he tried to control it, wanting to do this.
Right in the fire-stick his semen suddenly fell; as it was churned there, Shuka, of great austerity, was born.
The supreme sage, great yogi, born from the fire-stick's womb: as kindled fire shines, having received the offering,
so Shuka was born, blazing as it were with brilliance, bearing, O best of Brahmins, a form and colour wonderful and unsurpassed.
The Ganga, best of rivers, in her own form on Meru's back, came to him and bathed him with her water, O Narada.
A black antelope skin fell from the sky to the ground for Shuka; Gandharvas sang and Apsaras danced;
the divine drums sounded with great noise; Vishvavasu the Gandharva, Tumburu and Narada,
Haha and Huhu praised the birth of Shuka. There Shakra and the guardians of the world assembled,
gods, divine sages and Brahmin sages too; the wind rained all divine flowers.
The moving and unmoving world became joyful. The great-souled, radiant lord himself, with the Goddess, out of affection
initiated the sage's newborn son by rule; and Indra, lord of the gods, gave him a divine, wondrous-looking
water-pot with love, and the gods gave clothing all around; swans, lotuses-birds and thousands of cranes
circled him to the right, and parrots and chasha birds, O Narada. The great sage who then took a divine birth in the fire-stick
stayed right there, wise, observing vows, attentive. As soon as he was born the Vedas with their secrets and compendia
attended that best of sages as they did his father. He chose Brihaspati, knower of the Vedas, Vedangas and commentaries,
as his teacher, O best of Brahmins, reflecting only on dharma. Having studied all the Vedas with their secrets and compendia,
and the epics in full, and the Vedic scriptures all around, the great sage, having given the teacher's fee, returned.
He began fierce austerity as a celibate student, attentive; even in childhood, a sage of great austerity of gods and sages.
He was to be consulted and was born for knowledge and austerity; his mind did not delight in the stages of life, O lord of sages.
Seeing the dharma of liberation in the three householder-roots, Shuka, reflecting only on liberation, went to his father.
Having saluted him, he said with humility, wishing for the best: "May the Lord, skilled in the dharmas of liberation, tell me
how supreme peace of mind may arise, O sage." Hearing his son's words, the great sage said to him:
Study the scripture of liberation and the various dharmas. By his father's order Shuka, best of knowers of Brahman, took them up,
the entire scripture of yoga and the Kapila (Sankhya), O Narada, a hundred, endowed with Brahmic glory and Brahma-like valour.
Vyasa considered his son expert in the scriptures of liberation. He then said, "Go to Janaka, lord of Mithila.
That king will tell you in full about liberation." By his father's order he went to King Janaka of Mithila
to ask about the ultimate of dharma and the supreme refuge of liberation. "Go thus, unastonished, when addressed by a man;
do not go by your power, moving through the sky; you should go with simplicity, not for ease in a moment.
Distinctions are not to be seen, for they are of the attached. Do not be proud before that king, who is worthy of sacrifice.
Stay in his dwelling; he will cut your doubt. That king is skilled in dharma and expert in the scriptures of liberation.
Whatever he tells you, do without hesitation." Thus told, the righteous sage went to Mithila.
On foot — though able to cross the earth with its oceans through the sky — passing mountains too, he reached the land of Bharata.
The great sage, passing various prosperous countries, reached Videha and met Janaka.
Having reached the palace gate, stopped by the gatekeepers, the great yogi stood there, free of hunger and thirst,
free of weariness in the sun, intent on meditation, O Narada. One of those gatekeepers stationed there,
seeing Shuka standing like the sun at noon, honoured him properly, saluted with folded hands,
and let him into the second enclosure of the royal house. There, connected to the inner apartments, a great (garden) like Chaitraratha,
with well-divided water-play, lovely, with flowering trees, showing him, he seated him and informed the king.
Hearing that Shuka had come, the king appointed courtesans to serve him and to learn his state of mind, O best of sages.
Those fair-haired, graceful, young women of pleasant look, clad in fine red cloth and ornamented with refined gold,
skilled in conversation, knowers of moods, expert in all, over fifty of them, prepared water for the feet and other services.
They satisfied him with excellent food suited to place and time. When he had eaten, dear one, they then showed him
the lovely city-garden, one by one, O Narada; playing, laughing and singing they attended Shuka.
All of them, knowing character, attended that noble-natured one. But the son of the fire-stick, pure-souled, victor over anger and the senses,
ever in meditation, neither rejoices nor is angered. Having washed his feet and performed the twilight worship, Shuka
sat on a holy seat and reflected on that very matter. In the first part of the night he was intent on meditation,
at midnight the lord took sleep as is proper. Then rising in the morning and performing purification,
surrounded by women, the wise one took up meditation only. By this method there the rest of that day too
and that night he spent in the king's house, O Narada.
As a tortoise stretches out its limbs and draws them in again, so the monk should restrain the senses by the mind.
As what lies in darkness is seen by a lamp, so the Self can be seen by the lamp of the intellect.
I see all this in you, O best of the wise; and whatever else is to be known, you know in truth.
O Brahmin sage, you are known; you have reached the end of objects, by your teacher's grace and your instruction.
By his grace divine knowledge has arisen in the great sage, blazing; by that you are known, known to me.
Your knowledge is greater, your attainment greater, your lordship greater — and this you do not realise.
Through childhood, doubt, fear, or ignorance, even when knowledge has arisen they do not reach that goal.
By pure resolve, those like me, whose doubts are cut, loosening the knots of the heart, attain that state.
You, with knowledge arisen, steady-minded and without greed, without resolve, O Brahmin, will not attain that state.
For you there is no distinction in pleasure and pain, none in things; no eagerness for dance and song, no passion arises.
No bondage in kinsmen, no fear in fears; I see you, O fortunate one, equal to blame and praise of yourself.
I see you, and the other wise ones too, established on the supreme path, imperishable and faultless.
The fruit here for a Brahmin whose aim is liberation and whose state is calamitous — in that you stand. What else do you ask, O Brahmin?
Sanandana said: Hearing these words, with a perfected self and certain resolve, abiding in the Self by the Self and seeing the Self by the Self,
his duty done, happy and peaceful, he went silently northward. Reaching the snowy mountain he saw Vyasa, son of Parashara,
teaching his disciples Paila and others the Vedic collections. The pure-souled son of the fire-stick, radiant as the sun,
took his father's feet respectfully, with a glad mind, and then the noble-minded one told his father everything,
his dialogue with King Janaka, a means of liberation. Hearing it, the maker of the Veda, with a delighted heart,
embraced his son and made him sit at his side.
Then Paila and the other Brahmins, having studied the Vedas from Vyasa, came down from the peak, devoted to sacrificing and teaching.
Then the best of knowers said to Shuka, O Brahmin: "What are you doing, O fortunate son of Vyasa, great in radiance?"
Shuka said: "I am engaged in study, O son of Brahma, and now I stand here; I have come to see you by some merit.
I wish to ask you something: the truth, the means of liberation. Tell me, O fortunate one, how I may attain that knowledge."
Sanatkumara said: "There is no eye like knowledge, no austerity like knowledge; no sorrow like attachment, no happiness like renunciation.
Turning away from sinful action, constant merit, good conduct and right behaviour: this is the unsurpassed good.
Having obtained joyless human birth, he who clings is deluded; attachment, whose mark is sorrow, does not suffice for release from sorrow.
For one who clings, the intellect becomes the spreader of the net of delusion; covered by the net of delusion, he gets sorrow here and hereafter.
By every means desire and anger must be restrained by one seeking the good; for they are bent on destroying the good.
One should always protect austerity from anger, prosperity from envy, learning from honour and dishonour, and the self from negligence.
Gentleness is the highest dharma, forbearance the greatest strength, knowledge of the Self the highest knowledge, truth the greatest good.
He who has given up everything is a knower and a wise man, moving here with the senses under his own control among the objects of the senses,
unattached, tranquil, changeless, collected, with and without (the senses) that have become his Self.
He, freed, soon reaches the highest good: not seeing, not touching, and likewise not speaking, always with beings...
one gains the great good, O sage. He should not injure any beings; he should live in friendliness with beings.
Having obtained this birth, one should not make enmity with anyone. Poverty, contentment, freedom from expectation and steadiness:
these they call the highest good for the knower of the Self, self-conquered. Giving up possessions, my dear, become master of the senses.
Take refuge in a griefless state, fearless here and hereafter. The expectation-free do not grieve; give up expectations of yourself.
Having given up expectations, gentle one, you will be freed from the village of sorrow, by a sage constantly austere, self-controlled, and restrained.
One who desires to conquer the unconquered should be unattached amid attachments, unattached to the qualities and their attachments, always delighting in solitary conduct.
The Brahmin soon attains unsurpassed happiness. A wretched sage delights among beings who play in dualities.
He is content with a little wisdom; content with knowledge, he does not grieve. By auspicious acts one gains godhood; by mixed ones, a human birth;
and by inauspicious deeds, helpless, a lower birth. Constantly pursued there by sorrows of death and old age,
the creature sees samsara; why do you not understand? You take the harmful as beneficial, the impermanent as permanent,
and the useless as useful; why do you not understand? Wrapped by many threads of delusion made by your own offspring,
you do not understand, wrapped like a silkworm. Enough of possessions here; possession is faulty.
A silkworm is bound by its own possession. Creatures attached to son, wife and family sink,
like old forest elephants sunk in a lake of mud. See the creatures, much distressed, dragged by the net of delusion.
Family, son, wife, body, and heap of wealth are all another's and impermanent: what is one's own? Good and evil deeds.
When everything must be abandoned and you must go helpless, why are you attached to the useless and do not follow your own good?
Without rest, without support, without provisions, without a guide, making darkness — how will you go alone on that road?
No one will follow you from behind when you depart; only your good and evil deeds will follow you as you go.
Learning, action, valour and extensive knowledge are taught for the sake of wealth; but one who has attained the goal is freed.
This rope that binds is the delight of one who lives in a village; those of good deeds cut it and go; evildoers do not cut it.
You see those equal in birth, age and form carried off by death; yet no disgust arises: your heart is iron.
The river whose banks are form, whose current is the mind, whose islands are touch, which carries tastes, whose mud is smell, whose water is sound, hard to climb on the road to heaven —
one should cross with the boat of intellect, having forbearance as oars, made of truth, firmness in dharma as its rudder, swift with renunciation as its wind.
Giving up dharma and adharma, give up both truth and falsehood. Give up dharma by absence of resolve, and adharma by non-violence;
having given up both truth and falsehood with the supreme resolve of intellect — this body with pillars of bone, bound with sinews, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, foul-smelling, filled with urine and faeces, afflicted with old age and grief, a dwelling of disease, unsteady —
menstruating and impermanent, the dwelling of the elements: abandon it. This whole world, moving and unmoving as well, whatever there is,
all is made of the great elements, with atoms from it. The five senses, and tamas, sattva and rajas —
this is the group of seventeen, called the heap (rashi) of the unmanifest, with all sense-objects, manifest and unmanifest, for benefit.
The group of twenty-five, made of manifest and unmanifest: united with all these it is called impermanent.
The three aims, pleasure, pain, life and death — he who knows this truly knows origin and dissolution.
What is grasped by the senses is called manifest; the unmanifest is to be known as grasped by inference, beyond the senses.
The embodied one is satisfied by the controlled senses as if by streams; he sees the world prescribed in the Self, and the Self in the world.
The power of the one who sees the higher and lower does not see the time-limit of knowledge, seeing all beings in all conditions always.
For one who has become Brahman, union with the inauspicious does not occur; through knowledge, there is no return of the various afflictions born of the body.
By the light of the world's intellect the world's path is not harmed. The creature, beginningless and endless, imperishable, resides in the Self,
not a doer, not deluded, said the Lord, knower of the fords. The creature that is constantly unhappy by his own acts,
to counter his own suffering, injures in many ways. Then he takes up much other new karma,
and is tormented again by it, like a patient who ate what is unwholesome. Constantly, ending in delusion, he thinks of sorrows as pleasure,
is bound and tormented always by fearful deeds. Then, turned back from bondage, by the rise of his own acts here,
he wanders in samsara like a wheel without arms; by restraint, by turning from attachments, by the power of austerity...
